wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for spiced apple rings: tart apple rings cooked in a sweet syrup with vinegar, cloves and cinnamon, hot packed and processed in a boiling-water bath. [T:SLO-620,SLO-622,SLO-623]

akapity: NCHFP calls this an older USDA recipe that is still available and valid, but with an extremely high sugar concentration that most people today do not like. [T:SLO-621]
NCHFP is working on an updated version for next year and says you might want to wait and not try this version. [T:SLO-621]
This catalogue variant, apples in a spiced vinegar brine, is covered here only by this recipe: apple rings in a sweet spiced syrup with vinegar. [T:SLO-620,SLO-622]

sekcje.naglowek: Why you must not change the recipe
akapity: The FDA list gives eating apples a pH of about 3.30–4.00. [T:ACI-126]
NCHFP keeps its apple recipes but advises using fresh, sound apples, and if you are unsure of their pH, refrigerate or freeze apple products instead of storing them at room temperature. [T:SLO-048]
The whole product must contain a minimum, uniform level of acid so that botulism bacteria cannot grow. [T:ACI-017]
Do not change the proportions of vinegar, fruit and water and do not use vinegar of unknown acidity; use only recipes with tested proportions. [T:ACI-016]
JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not change the amounts of vinegar, apples or water and do not add other vegetables; the recipe is tested only in the proportions given. [T:ACI-265]
White distilled vinegar and cider vinegar of 5% acidity are recommended for pickles. [T:ACI-018]
Penn State Extension advises vinegar of 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and advises against diluting vinegar with water unless a research-tested recipe says so. [T:ACI-209,ACI-210]

JarAtlas rule (cautious, for readers outside the USA): use the white distilled (spirit) vinegar the recipe lists, labelled 5% or 6% acidity; do not use 10% vinegar and do not dilute it with water to make 5% vinegar; add only the water the recipe lists. [T:ACI-211,ACI-018]
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml. [T:ACI-195]

For about 8 to 9 pint jars NCHFP lists 12 pounds (about 5.4 kg) of firm, tart apples with a diameter of at most 2 1/2 inches (about 6.4 cm), 12 cups of sugar, 6 cups of water and 1 1/4 cups of white vinegar (5%). [T:SLO-620]
Spices: 3 tablespoons of whole cloves and 3/4 cup of red hot cinnamon candies or 8 cinnamon sticks; NCHFP also lists 1 teaspoon of red food coloring as optional. [T:SLO-620]
If you cannot get the cinnamon candies, use the cinnamon sticks that the recipe gives as the alternative. [T:SLO-620]
Wash the apples. [T:SLO-622]

To prevent discoloration, peel and slice one apple at a time: immediately cut it crosswise into 1/2-inch (about 1.3 cm) slices, remove the core area with a melon baller and put the rings into an ascorbic acid solution. [T:SLO-622]

NCHFP makes this solution from 3 g (3000 mg) of ascorbic acid per 1 gallon (about 3.8 l) of cold water: 1 level teaspoon of pure powder weighs about 3 g, or you can crush and dissolve 6 vitamin C tablets of 500 mg per gallon of water. [T:SLO-626]
For commercial mixes of ascorbic and citric acid, follow the manufacturer's directions. [T:SLO-626]
Combine the sugar, water, vinegar, cloves, cinnamon candies or cinnamon sticks and food coloring in a 6-quart (about 5.7 l) saucepan. [T:SLO-622]
Stir, heat to boiling and simmer for 3 minutes. [T:SLO-622]
Drain the apples, add them to the hot syrup and cook for 5 minutes. [T:SLO-622]
Fill the jars, preferably wide-mouth, with the apple rings and hot syrup, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace. [T:SLO-622]
Put on the lids and process. [T:SLO-622]
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars in a boiling-water bath for 10 minutes. [T:SLO-623,ACI-176]
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased. [T:ACI-015]
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process them for 15 minutes. [T:SLO-624,ACI-176]
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 20 minutes. [T:SLO-625,ACI-176]
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m. [T:ACI-176]
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage. [T:ACI-015]
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint and pint jars. [T:SLO-623]
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml. [T:ACI-179,ACI-174]
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures. [T:SLO-210]

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed. [T:SLO-196,SLO-212]

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home. [T:SLO-223,SLO-212]
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use this card only with jars that take two-piece canning lids; it gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids, so do not use them for this recipe. [T:SLO-223]
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed. [T:SLO-196]
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days. [T:SLO-197]

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil. [T:SLO-198]
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre. [T:SLO-191]
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour. [T:SLO-191]
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid. [T:SLO-191]
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage. [T:SLO-190]
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar. [T:SLO-190]
